title: Changing the subject
objectives: Rearrange a formula to make a different letter the subject
Rearrange a formula where the subject appears twice

screens.prose: Simple interest on a loan follows a formula: $$I = Prt$$ $P$ is the amount borrowed in pounds, $r$ the yearly rate as a decimal and $t$ the years. $I$ is the interest.
screens.question: Fill in the interest, in pounds, for each loan.

hints.text: Multiply the three numbers in each row.
Row one: $2000 \times 0.05 = 100$ a year.
Then times 3 years: £300.00. Do the same for the other rows.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $P$, $r$ and $t$ in each row.

byKey.r0c3: Row one: $2000 \times 0.05 \times 3$. A year's interest is £100.00, so three years is £300.00.
byKey.r1c3: Row two: $1500 \times 0.04 \times 2$. A year's interest is £60.00.
byKey.r2c3: Row three: $800 \times 0.025 \times 4$. A year's interest is £20.00.

explain.text: Putting numbers in place of letters is substituting, as in l1. Each row is $P \times r \times t$: for example $2000 \times 0.05 \times 3 = 300$. The formula gives $I$ directly because $I$ stands alone on one side.

screens.prose: Take the first loan: £2,000.00 at 0.05 a year. Slide the years $t$. The line is marked in pounds of interest, so the point shows $I$.
screens.question: How many years does the loan take to build up £250.00 of interest?

hints.text: How much interest does one year add?
Each year moves the point £100.00 along.
£250.00 is two and a half lots of £100.00.

feedback.correct: 2.5 years: £100.00 a year, so £250.00 takes two and a half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one year's interest, then count how many fit into £250.00.

byKey.principal: You divided £250.00 by £2,000.00. Divide by one year's interest, $2000 \times 0.05$.
byKey.rate: You divided £250.00 by 0.05. Divide by the whole year's interest, $2000 \times 0.05 = 100$.

explain.text: One year adds $2000 \times 0.05 = 100$ pounds, so you divided 250 by 100 to get 2.5 years. In letters you divided $I$ by $P \times r$. That is a new formula with $t$ alone: $t = \dfrac{I}{Pr}$.

screens.prose: The letter alone on one side is the formula's **subject**. In $I = Prt$ the subject is $I$. **Changing the subject** means rearranging, with equation moves, until another letter stands alone.
screens.question: Make $t$ the subject of $I = Prt$.

ops.label: Subtract $Pr$ from both sides
ops.why: $Pr$ multiplies $t$; it is not added to it. Undo a multiplication by dividing.

hints.text: What is being done to $t$ on the right?
$t$ is multiplied by $P$ and by $r$. Undo both at once.
Divide both sides by $Pr$, then write $t$ on the left.

feedback.correct: $t = \dfrac{I}{Pr}$, the rule you used on the line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the multiplication by dividing both sides.

byKey.w1: You subtracted $Pr$. But $t$ is multiplied by $Pr$, so divide instead.

explain.text: Dividing both sides by $Pr$ leaves $t$ alone. The new formula is exactly what you did on the line: interest over one year's interest. Check: $\dfrac{250}{2000 \times 0.05} = 2.5$.

screens.prose: A train covers $d$ km in $t$ hours at a speed of $s$ km/h, so $s = \dfrac{d}{t}$. This time the letter you want sits under a fraction line.
screens.question: Make $t$ the subject of $s = \dfrac{d}{t}$.

ops.label: Multiply both sides by $d$
ops.why: That leaves $t$ under the fraction line. Multiply by $t$ to clear it.

ops.label: Subtract $d$ from both sides
ops.why: $d$ is divided by $t$, not added. Subtracting cannot free $t$.

ops.label: Divide both sides by $d$
ops.why: Dividing by $d$ leaves $\dfrac{st}{d} = 1$, and $t$ is still tied to $s$. Divide by $s$.

hints.text: First get $t$ off the bottom of the fraction.
Multiplying both sides by $t$ gives $st = d$.
Now $t$ is multiplied by $s$. Divide both sides by $s$.

feedback.correct: $t = \dfrac{d}{s}$. Check: 240 km at 80 km/h takes 3 hours.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Clear the fraction first, then divide.

byKey.w1: Multiplying by $d$ leaves $t$ under the line. Multiply by $t$ instead.
byKey.w2: Subtracting $d$ does not free $t$, because $d$ is divided by $t$.
byKey.w3: Dividing by $d$ leaves $t$ tied to $s$. Divide by $s$ to free it.

explain.text: Multiplying by $t$ lifts it off the bottom: $st = d$. Then dividing by $s$ frees it: $t = \dfrac{d}{s}$. Two moves, undone in reverse order of how $t$ was trapped.

screens.prose: A stall sells mugs at a price $p$ of £9.50. Each costs $c$ = £5.50 to make, and rent is $F$ = £1,200.00 a month. Profit on $q$ mugs is $q(p - c) - F$. Break-even, as in l9, is where profit is 0.
screens.question: How many mugs must the stall sell to break even?

hints.text: Set $0 = q(p - c) - F$ and make $q$ the subject.
Add $F$ to both sides: $F = q(p - c)$. Each mug adds $p - c$ to profit.
Divide by the bracket: $q = \dfrac{F}{p - c} = \dfrac{1200}{9.50 - 5.50}$.

feedback.correct: 300 mugs. Each one adds £4.00, and 300 × £4.00 covers the £1,200.00 rent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make $q$ the subject, then substitute.

byKey.price-only: You divided by the price, £9.50. Each mug only adds $p - c$, which is £4.00, to profit.
byKey.cost-only: You divided by the cost, £5.50. Divide by the margin per mug, $p - c$.
byKey.added: You divided by $p + c$. The bracket is $p - c$: price minus cost.

explain.text: From $0 = q(p - c) - F$, add $F$ and divide by the bracket: $q = \dfrac{F}{p - c}$. Each mug earns £4.00 over its cost, so $\dfrac{1200}{4} = 300$. The table agrees: profit climbs £400.00 per 100 mugs from −£800.00.

screens.prose: A data plan costs £5.00 a month plus £2.00 per gigabyte, so $C = 5 + 2n$ for $n$ gigabytes.
screens.question: Which formula makes $n$ the subject?

options.why: You divided $C$ by 2 but not the 5. Test $C = 11$: you get 0.5, not 3.
You added 5. The formula adds 5 to $2n$, so undo it by subtracting. Test $C = 11$: you get 8.
You halved the 5 and left $C$ whole. Dividing must reach every term. Test $C = 11$: you get 8.5.

hints.text: How was $C$ built from $n$? Doubled first, then 5 added.
Test a row: when $C = 11$, $n$ must come out as 3.
Undo in reverse order: subtract 5, then divide all of $C - 5$ by 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the last step first, and divide every term.

byKey.one-term: You divided only $C$ by 2. Test $C = 11$: $\dfrac{11}{2} - 5 = 0.5$, not 3.
byKey.added: You added 5 instead of taking it away. Test $C = 11$: you get 8, not 3.
byKey.order: You halved the 5 but not $C$. Test $C = 11$: you get 8.5, not 3.

explain.text: $C$ was built by doubling $n$, then adding 5. Undo in reverse: subtract 5 to get $C - 5 = 2n$, then divide the whole of $C - 5$ by 2. Testing a row from the table catches a wrong rearrangement at once.

screens.prose: A trade's return is $r = \dfrac{P_1 - P_0}{P_0}$, where $P_0$ is the entry price and $P_1$ the exit. To find the entry from the exit, make $P_0$ the subject. It appears twice, so we gather it, then factorise.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $rP_0 = P_1 - P_0$, multiply both sides by $P_0$
$rP_0 + P_0 = P_1$, add $P_0$ to both sides
$P_0(1 + r) = P_1$, take out the common factor $P_0$
$P_0 = \dfrac{P_1}{1 + r}$, divide both sides by $1 + r$

hints.text: Clear the fraction first.
Once both $P_0$ terms are on one side, take $P_0$ out as a factor.
Multiply by $P_0$, add $P_0$, factorise, divide by $1 + r$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line must follow from the one before by one move.

byKey.c: Factorising needs both $P_0$ terms on the same side. Add $P_0$ first.
byKey.d: You can only divide by $1 + r$ once $P_0$ is a single factor.

explain.text: With $P_0$ in two places, no single move frees it. Gathering both on one side and factorising turns them into one $P_0$. Check: an exit of £55.00 after a return of 0.10 gives $\dfrac{55}{1.1} = 50$.

screens.prose: Three trades from a backtest log lost their entry prices. Use $P_0 = \dfrac{P_1}{1 + r}$.
screens.question: Fill in each entry price, in pounds.

hints.text: Work out $1 + r$ for each trade first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each exit price by $1 + r$.

byKey.r0c3: Trade A: $\dfrac{52.50}{1.05} = 50.00$. Taking 5% off £52.50 gives £49.88, which is wrong: the 5% was measured from the entry.
byKey.r1c3: Trade B lost money, so $1 + r = 0.96$ and the entry was higher than the exit: $\dfrac{38.40}{0.96}$.

explain.text: Each entry is the exit divided by $1 + r$: £50.00, £40.00 and £110.00. Trade B fell 4%, so its entry sits above its exit. Taking $r$ off the exit price instead gives the wrong answer, because returns are measured from the entry.

screens.prose: A broker sets the margin on $q$ shares at price $p$ as $M = mpq$, with margin rate $m$. You have $M$ = £6,000.00 for margin, the rate is $m = 0.25$, and the price is $p$ = £48.00.
screens.question: What is the largest number of shares you can buy?

hints.text: Make $q$ the subject first.
$q$ is multiplied by $m$ and by $p$. Divide by both.
$q = \dfrac{M}{mp} = \dfrac{6000}{0.25 \times 48}$.

feedback.correct: 500 shares. Each one needs £12.00 of margin.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make $q$ the subject, then substitute.

byKey.no-rate: You divided £6,000.00 by the full price. With margin you only put up 25% of it, £12.00 a share.
byKey.times-rate: You multiplied by the rate. It sits beside $q$ in $mpq$, so divide by it.
byKey.all-times: You multiplied everything together. Undo the multiplications by dividing.

explain.text: Dividing both sides of $M = mpq$ by $mp$ gives $q = \dfrac{M}{mp}$. Each share needs $0.25 \times 48 = 12$ pounds of margin. So £6,000.00 covers $\dfrac{6000}{12} = 500$ shares.

ideas: The subject is the letter alone on one side. Substituting into it gives that letter directly.
To change the subject, undo what was done to the letter, in reverse order, to both sides.
If the letter appears twice, gather both on one side and take it out as a factor.

formula.name: Entry price from a return
formula.tex: r = \dfrac{P_1 - P_0}{P_0} \;\text{ rearranges to }\; P_0 = \dfrac{P_1}{1 + r}
formula.note: Test any rearrangement with one row of numbers.

summary.trap: Divide every term, not just one: from $C = 5 + 2n$, $n = \dfrac{C - 5}{2}$, not $\dfrac{C}{2} - 5$.

options.why: You subtracted $Pt$. But $r$ is multiplied by $Pt$, so divide.
That is upside down. Dividing both sides of $I = Prt$ by $Pt$ puts $I$ on top.
You multiplied instead of dividing. Undo a multiplication by dividing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the multiplication.

explain.text: $r$ is multiplied by $P$ and $t$. Dividing both sides by $Pt$ leaves $r = \dfrac{I}{Pt}$.

quiz.prose: A formula from physics: $v = u + at$.
quiz.question: Which formula makes $a$ the subject?

options.why: You divided $v$ by $t$ but not $u$. Subtract $u$ first, then divide everything.
You added $u$. It is added to $at$, so subtract it.
You subtracted $t$. But $t$ multiplies $a$, so divide by it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the last step first.

explain.text: $a$ was multiplied by $t$, then $u$ was added. Undo in reverse: $v - u = at$, then $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$.

quiz.prose: A position was closed at £66.00 for a return of 0.10.
quiz.question: What was the entry price?

byKey.off-exit: You took 10% off £66.00. The 10% was measured from the entry, so divide by 1.10.
byKey.times: You multiplied by 1.10. To go back from exit to entry, divide.

quiz.question: Which formula makes the price $p$ the subject?

options.why: You subtracted $c$. From $p - c = \dfrac{F}{q}$, add $c$ to both sides.
You moved $c$ before clearing the fraction, and with the wrong sign. Multiply by $p - c$ first.
You multiplied $F$ by $q$. From $q(p - c) = F$, divide both sides by $q$ instead.

feedback.correct: $p = \dfrac{F}{q} + c$: the cost plus each unit's share of the rent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Clear the fraction, divide by $q$, then add $c$.

explain.text: Multiply by $p - c$: $q(p - c) = F$. Divide by $q$: $p - c = \dfrac{F}{q}$. Add $c$: $p = \dfrac{F}{q} + c$.
